los.text: Evaluate the patency of a patient’s airway in clinical scenarios
los.html:
AssessSigns of obstruction
LookSee-saw breathing (chest and abdomen moving in opposite directions), accessory muscles, cyanosis, foreign body, vomit, swelling
ListenStridor (upper airway), snoring (tongue/soft palate), gurgling (fluid), hoarseness; silence in complete obstruction
FeelAir movement at the mouth
  • A talking patient has a patent airway (for now).
  • Causes: reduced consciousness (tongue falls back), vomit, blood, foreign body, anaphylaxis, burns, trauma.

los.text: Perform a head tilt chin lift manoeuvre to open a patient’s airway safely
los.html:
1Place one hand on the forehead and tilt the head back.
2Put the fingertips of the other hand under the bony point of the chin and lift.
3Avoid pressing on the soft tissues under the chin.
  • Avoid in suspected cervical spine injury: use a jaw thrust instead.

los.text: Demonstrate a jaw thrust technique to manage an obstructed airway
los.html:
1Kneel behind the patient's head.
2Place your fingers behind the angles of the mandible on both sides.
3Push the jaw forwards and upwards, using the thumbs on the chin to open the mouth slightly.
  • Use when: possible cervical spine injury (keeps the neck neutral) or when head tilt chin lift fails.

los.text: Demonstrate the correct technique to measure and insert an oropharyngeal airway in a clinical scenario
los.html:
StepDetail
IndicationUnconscious patient with no gag reflex
SizingFrom the incisors to the angle of the jaw
Insertion (adults)Insert upside down (concave side up) into the mouth, slide to the soft palate, then rotate 180° and advance
Insertion (children)Insert the right way up using a tongue depressor
CheckAirway improved; reassess breathing
Remove ifGagging or coughing (risk of vomiting and laryngospasm)

los.text: Demonstrate the correct technique to measure and insert a nasopharyngeal airway in a clinical scenario
los.html:
StepDetail
IndicationReduced consciousness but gag reflex present, clenched jaw (e.g. seizures)
SizingFrom the tip of the nose to the tragus of the ear; width roughly the patient's little finger
Insertion
  • Lubricate
  • Insert into the right nostril (usually)
  • Bevel facing the septum
  • Straight back along the nasal floor (not upwards)
  • with a gentle twist
ContraindicationSuspected base of skull fracture (relative), severe facial trauma
CheckAirway improved; watch for nosebleed

los.text: Evaluate a patient's breathing pattern to identify abnormalities
los.html:
• Look: rate, depth, pattern, accessory muscles, recession, chest symmetry, cyanosis, ability to speak in sentences.
PatternSeen in
TachypnoeaPneumonia, PE, asthma, metabolic acidosis, sepsis
BradypnoeaOpioids, raised intracranial pressure, exhaustion
Kussmaul (deep, sighing)Diabetic ketoacidosis
Cheyne–Stokes (waxing and waning with apnoeas)Heart failure, stroke, near death
Prolonged expiration, wheezeAsthma, COPD
Paradoxical / see-sawAirway obstruction, flail chest
  • Then: expansion, percussion, auscultation, saturations.

los.text: Measure and record a patient’s respiratory rate accurately
los.html:
• Count for a full 60 seconds (or 30 × 2 if regular), ideally without the patient knowing (e.g. while still "taking the pulse").
  • Normal adult: 12–20 breaths/min. NEWS2: 21–24 scores 2; ≤8 or ≥25 scores 3.
  • Record the rate, any distress, and on oxygen what device and flow.

los.text: Measure and interpret oxygen saturation levels using pulse oximetry
los.html:
• Technique: probe on a warm finger (or earlobe), wait for a good waveform, remove nail varnish, keep the hand still.
TargetPatient
94–98%Most acutely ill patients
88–92%Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease)
  • Limitations: poor perfusion, cold, movement, nail varnish, carbon monoxide (falsely normal), darker skin (can overestimate).
    • Saturations don't show CO₂ retention: check an ABG.

los.text: Identify clinical indications for administering supplementary oxygen
los.html:
• Indication: hypoxaemia (sats below target), not breathlessness alone (BTS guideline).
SituationOxygen
Critical illness (cardiac arrest, shock, sepsis, anaphylaxis, major trauma)15 L/min via non-rebreather mask at first
Acutely ill with low satsTitrate to 94–98%
At risk of hypercapnia (COPD)Venturi 24–28%, target 88–92%; check an ABG
Not hypoxic (e.g. uncomplicated MI, stroke)Not needed
  • Oxygen is a drug: it must be prescribed with a target range.

los.text: Evaluate a patient’s circulation during clinical assessment
los.html:
AssessLook for
LookPallor, mottling, sweating, bleeding, JVP
FeelHands: warm or cold, capillary refill (press the fingertip for 5 s at heart level: normal <2 s), pulse rate and character
MeasureBlood pressure, heart rate
ListenHeart sounds
OtherUrine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), fluid balance
  • Shock: tachycardia, cool peripheries, prolonged CRT, hypotension (late), low urine output, confusion.

los.text: Measure and interpret manual blood pressure readings accurately
los.html:
1Patient seated and rested for 5 minutes, arm supported at heart level, no tight clothing.
2Choose the correct cuff size (bladder covers ~80% of the arm circumference).
3Estimate systolic by palpation: inflate until the radial pulse disappears, add 20–30 mmHg.
4Inflate to that level, place the stethoscope over the brachial artery, deflate at 2–3 mmHg per second.
5. SystolicFirst sound (Korotkoff I); diastolic = disappearance (Korotkoff V).
ReadingMeaning
<90 systolicHypotension
≥140/90 (clinic)Possible hypertension → confirm with ambulatory or home readings
≥180/120Severe: same-day assessment if symptoms or organ damage
  • Errors: small cuff (falsely high), arm below heart level (high), talking, rounding to zero.

los.text: Measure and record a patient’s pulse using appropriate technique
los.html:
• Radial pulse: two fingers (not thumb) lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon
    • count for 60 seconds (or 30 × 2 if regular).
AssessNormal / abnormal
Rate60–100/min; <60 bradycardia, >100 tachycardia
RhythmRegular, regularly irregular, irregularly irregular (AF)
Volume and characterUse the carotid for character: slow-rising (aortic stenosis), collapsing (aortic regurgitation)
Radio-radial delaySubclavian stenosis, aortic dissection
Radio-femoral delayCoarctation

los.text: Assess and interpret a patient's level of consciousness using CAVPU
los.html:
CAVPUMeaning
Confusion (new)New confusion or delirium: scores 3 on NEWS2
AlertAwake, eyes open spontaneously
VoiceResponds to voice
PainResponds only to a painful stimulus (e.g. trapezius squeeze)
UnresponsiveNo response
  • P or U roughly equals GCS ≤8: the airway is at risk, so get senior and anaesthetic help.
  • Then: check glucose, pupils, consider GCS for more detail.

los.text: Evaluate pupillary response to light and its clinical significance during a clinical examination
los.html:
• Technique: dim the light
    • ask the patient to look into the distance
    • shine a pen torch into each eye from the side: check the direct and consensual responses
    • size (mm)
    • shape
    • symmetry.
FindingSuggests
Pinpoint pupilsOpioids, pontine haemorrhage
Fixed dilated pupil (one side)Third nerve compression (uncal herniation, PCom aneurysm): emergency
Bilateral fixed dilatedSevere brain injury, anticholinergics, death
Small reactive pupil with ptosisHorner's syndrome
Relative afferent pupillary defectOptic nerve disease

los.text: Recognise the importance of accurate blood glucose measurement in patient care
los.html:
• Always check capillary glucose ("Don't Ever Forget Glucose") in any patient with reduced consciousness, confusion, seizures or collapse.
LevelAction
<4 mmol/L (hypoglycaemia)Treat: oral fast-acting glucose if alert; IV 10–20% glucose or IM glucagon if not
4–7 mmol/LNormal (fasting)
>11 mmol/L with ketonesConsider DKA
  • Technique: clean the finger with water (sugar on the skin gives false highs)
    • use the side of the fingertip
    • discard the first drop if contaminated
    • check meter calibration and strip expiry.

los.text: Identify key clinical signs during the exposure phase of the primary survey in a clinical scenario
los.html:
Look forExample
TemperatureFever (sepsis), hypothermia
RashesNon-blanching purpuric rash (meningococcal sepsis), urticaria (anaphylaxis)
Bleeding / woundsHidden blood loss, trauma
SwellingCalf swelling (DVT), joint swelling
SkinPressure sores, injection marks, cellulitis
AbdomenDistension, tenderness
Lines and drainsInfection, output
  • Maintain dignity: expose only what you need, keep the patient warm, then cover up.

los.text: Differentiate between open and closed questioning in the context of patient history taking
los.html:
Open questionsClosed questions
Example"Tell me about the pain.""Is the pain worse when you breathe in?"
AnswerThe patient's own storyYes/no or a fact
UseStart of the consultation, exploring feelings, ICEClarifying details, red flags, systems review
AdvantageRich information, rapport, less biasQuick, precise
RiskCan be longMisses information, leading
  • Funnel: start open, then narrow down.

los.text: Use open-ended questions to facilitate the patient’s narrative during a consultation
los.html:
Examples"What brought you in today?", "Tell me more about that", "How has this affected you?"
ThenStay silent (the golden minute: let the patient talk), use facilitation (nodding, "go on"), echoing their words, and summarising.
AvoidInterrupting early and multiple questions at once.

los.text: Use closed questions to confirm or clarify clinical information during history taking
los.html:
Use toPin down details (onset, duration, severity), screen for red flags and complete the systems review.
Examples"When did it start?", "Have you lost weight?", "Do you smoke?"
Avoid leading questions ("You haven't had blood in your stool, have you?") and double questions ("Any cough or fever?").
